items.body: Earthworks is a travel set: a memoir of places visited, impressions gleaned and experiences translated into sound. Garling Wu and Jessie Leov composed the album remotely, folding in impressions of London, Japan, New Zealand and more. In the same way, the perfume that one may order along with the download is infused with orange blossom, ambergris, geranium and cypress. New Zealand’s Sandra McEvoy created the scent, Japanese artist Sayo Watano the cover and zine: a true international collaboration. Despite its many influences, the music is as unified as the cover collage. “Saline” begins with old-fashioned strings fed through new-fangled processing, receding to a series of synthetic dots. The music sparkles like sunlight on streams. A stuttering weather report offers glimpses of the day to come. The artists’ voices wander speaker-to-speaker over the sounds of water as the weather report grows clearer. A can is opened, producing an effervescent fizz. The music softens at the midway point. Solo piano opens a door to the second half, where flowing water meets encroaching wind. “Retreat” launches with that same piano; as Martin Roberts’ cello enters the frame, the timbre tilts from experimental to modern composition. The combination of this title and “All That Remains” hint at the album’s sub-theme of climate change. While the music celebrates the collected beauty of travel, it also suggests that the world’s wonders are as fragile as decaying piano notes. The opening chords of “All That Remains” ebb and flow as traffic speeds by, temporarily obscuring the now-improvised keys. Notes spin like tops, then fall over. The music bears a sense of encroachment; everything seems ready to collapse. Then Leov begins to sing of spirits, and the focus shifts from fracture to harmony: a gorgeous reclamation. “Sounding Bell” begins with solo, wordless voice, enhanced by intakes of breath. Placid crickets sing in the distance. The organic and electronic instruments both re-enter, working together in a spirit of cooperation. This time, in an act of generosity, even the passing car is given its own sonic space, while the train is well-integrated. “Sounding Bell” offers room to all, ringing said bell as an invitation, as holy ritual, as temple meditation. The album ends with a sense that disparate pieces have become one and a delicate balance has been restored. (Richard Allen)

items.body: From bubbling synths to irresistible basslines, Teleportations makes every stop on its cosmic journey worth visiting. Jamming through different galaxies Teleportations by Danalogue   I‘ve been a fan for a few years of both The Comet Is Coming (via The Leaf Label and Impulse! Records) and the fine UK-based Castles In Space imprint. Both of these names dabble in a type of electronica I’m definitely a fan of: very atmospheric music that does not shy away from being progressive as well. Danalogue, the core member handling the electronics for The Comet Is Coming, has now released his very first solo album under, you guessed it, Castles In Space—can’t get much more appropriate for me, can it? Teleportations is as groovy as it is conceptual. If you imagine yourself traveling through space and visiting different planets as the music plays, the experience will be greatly enhanced. The blend of futuristic synth-based pieces and robotic, sometimes unintelligible vocals calls back to a lot of ’80s space music and its hi-tech vision—though I’m sad to inform the ’80s that we still do not voyage through space; we tried our best. However, this record may help with that, because it’s an incredibly immersive LP despite its brevity. The tracks mostly flow into one another as a continuous mix, though each remains distinct; all ten pieces offer something either new or something that shakes up the previous atmosphere. Take “Moebius Tryptich” as an example, my favorite cut on the record. It is irresistibly groovy, and the drums are absolutely fantastic, starting off with a rather simple groove that becomes more complex as the tune progresses. In comparison to the previous “Far Beyond the Sun,” the lead single for the album, it’s almost night and day, yet the brief silence between them makes them flow really well. The first three tracks, of which “Far Beyond the Sun” is the last, seamlessly succeed one another instead, so that short silence between tracks three and four really does make a difference.   The three-track opening sequence is also noteworthy, especially the intro, “It’s Awakening On the Planet,” featuring bubbling arpeggiated synths. It’s really colorful and fun, and it pulls me in from the get-go. The transition between “Mother of Mars” and “Far Beyond the Sun” is also one of my favorite moments on the album because the arpeggiated synth that accompanies the former to its end then becomes one of the lead motifs of the latter. It’s rather awesome. Then follows the previously mentioned “Moebius Triptych,” a fantastic jam that I can’t get enough of. The bass on this tune may be my favorite part of the record; it’s so spectacularly groovy that I genuinely can’t stop playing it. In a similar fashion, “Theta Wave Convergence” and “Onto the Next Dimension” also go for a more energetic approach—and I don’t think it’s a coincidence that both also happen to be favorites of mine. The former is possibly the most peculiar track on the record, as it’s almost suitable for a club. The beat is classic house music, alternating a kick and a clap, but there’s also a really fast arpeggiated synth lead and techno-inspired hi-hats that make this tune as hypnotic as it is energetic. It also helps that there’s a neat breakdown in the middle with four-on-the-floor kicks, after which the piece builds up again with some acid synths. “Onto the Next Dimension” may be the fastest three minutes on the LP. A super-deep bass, clean percussion, and funk-inspired keyboard action make this the most fun cut. Though the whole album, both conceptually and musically, reminds me a lot of Flying Lotus, “Onto the Next Dimension” especially feels like something that could easily sneak onto “Cosmogramma” and no one would bat an eye. I hereby summon all Flying Lotus fans to check out this album, as I have no doubt they’d greatly appreciate it. A melancholic yet hopeful finale :: On the more atmospheric side of things, the futuristic vision of this LP shines even more. The closing “Earth Remembrance Day” sounds like a farewell to our home. After further review, it does not seem to be an actual holiday, which makes the whole record even cooler, almost as if our departure happened a long time ago and this piece serves as a proposed anthem to commemorate the event. The track is definitely fitting for that role. It is a melancholic yet hopeful finale, and for sure the most ’80s track of the bunch. It’s a great finisher, one that you could sneak into the final scene of a space film as some sort of goodbye. “You Are On The Right Track” is a sweet, interlude-like piece that keeps the momentum going, yet again spearheaded by layers of arpeggiated synths that feel like they never stop ascending. “Out Of Phase” welcomes you to some other world with an alien voice, which I cannot comprehend, though I’m sure it’s not because the vocals are unintelligible, but rather because it is an actual alien speaking in its own tongue. It’s small touches like this that make this LP as cool as it is, even if some imagination may be required from the listener. Teleportations is likely going to place as my number one “Coolest Record of the Year.” There’s such a wide variety of inspirations, from funk to space music, jazz drumming to lo-fi electronics, all fitting under such a neat space-travel experience. The concept ties all of this seemingly incompatible music together, making you imagine all sorts of different galaxies zooming by while occasionally letting you jam inside your spaceship. Music this dope does not come out every year, so Teleportations is a must-listen for fans of forward-thinking electronica. Teleportations is available on Castles In Space. [Bandcamp] Teleportations by Danalogue

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Clicked 5 stars, but really just close at 4.74 stars...I am returning to the Song-by-Song platform after a little break, with the latest album by Phideaux Xavier. The upstate New York progger has been recording and releasing music since 1992, with his first "proper" album coming in 1993 with "Feindish". This is the first album of all new material since 2018's "Infernal". I have heard and liked a number of his previous songs, but this will be my first listen to his upcoming album "AutoMoto Animus" which is due to be released on July 6, 2026. Phideaux is influenced by Jethro Tull, David Bowie, Pink Floyd, Van Der Graaf Generator, and early Genesis (among many others). This album comes courtesy of Anne-Claire Rallo of Bad Dog Promotions, but as always, I receive no additional compensation, and I call it like I hear it.While Phideaux plays many instruments and sings on the album, he has several special guests:Line-up / Musicians- Phideaux Xavier / piano, keyboards, bass, acoustic and electric guitar, vocalsWith:- Joe Berardi / drums- Dustin Boyer / guitar, synthesizers, claps- Ariel Farber / violin, viola, vocals- Roger Howarth / vocals- Amanda Lynne / flute- Vince Meghrouni / flute, piccolo, saxophone- Rich Mouser / guitar, keyboards, percussion- Charlie Paxson / drums, talking drum, tabla, percussion, tambourine- Fernando Perdomo / guitar- Savannah Pope / vocals- Kira Roessler / bass- Paul Roessler / drum programming, percussion, treatments, fancy piano, organ- Molly Ruttan / drums, vocals- Mark Sherkus / organ, mellotron- Naomi Adele Smith / keyboards, vocals- Johnny Unicorn / bass, vocals, whistle- Marcus Watkins / guitar, baritone guitar- Angus Weir / trumpets- Kaitlin Wolfberg / strings- Nathan York / bass- Juliet Mills / vocals- Marianne Muellerleile / vocals- Geoff Ball / vocalsLet's check it out!Track 1 - Do What You Will (4:46)This begins with a bit of a capella "aahs" before going into an almost "new wave" beat with sinister vocals that pan from side-to side. This is an introduction lyrically to what is to come. It seems to be a bit of a dystopian tale to come. I like the line "Welcome to reality, I hope you stay". There is a nice instrumental break before the second, very dramatic verse. The production on this is warm and rich, and the layers of sound are clean and distinguishable. In a perfect world, this song would get a lot of attention and be very popular as I believe its appeal goes way beyond that of the prog-fan niche. Fantastic track!Track 2 - Hey Humanity (4:13)The vocals and instruments begin simultaneously with an accent on the word "Hey". This one is slightly slower in tempo than the opener. It has a slightly Beatle-esque feel to it. At around 1:30, the vibe changes with the harmonised guitar solo. My goodness, the orchestration on this track is terrific! I also get a bit of ELO at their best from this track. This song is very melodic and engaging with lovely instrumental bits accentuating his vocals. I LOVE the guitar solo that happens near the end of the song! It is not a shredding or highly technical solo, but it works perfectly for the song. Another great track!Track 3 - Driving to Destruction (4:42)A driving piano rhythm with bass and drum accents and guitar on top starts this one off. Once again, I get ELO vibes. I love the sustained vocal note around 1:30. There are so many little pieces of ear candy in this arrangement! The harmony vocals are exquisite! The album's title features prominently in this one. Once again, the way the track "sounds" is very impressive. There seems to be a lot of attention to detail given to the production. Terrific song!Track 4 - Stay With Me (3:14)This is the album's shortest track. A synth note starts us out here. This one is a bit slower; something of a ballad, but not too slow. When the rhythm section kicks in it brings the song to a higher gear. The song builds in intensity. I feel the VDGG influence on this, but far more accessible to many listeners than Peter Hammill and company are known for. As has been the case, the production is amazing. I keep saying this, but want to be clear, these are strong songs to begin with, and the production is the icing on the cake. Killer track!Track 5 - Charlie Knew (4:05)This one begins with a big introduction before scaling back to piano and vocals with instrumental accents between the phrases. This is another beautifully arranged and orchestrated piece. I believe there is some saxophone on the choruses. If this album came out in the 70s or 80s it would be massive! Yet while the basic song structures would have fit in during that era, the production would be considered futuristic. Just one great track after another!Track 6 - Siren in the Storm (4:00)This one has a strumming acoustic guitar accompanying the vocals. There are some other touches adding color as well. Phideaux is spinning a wonderful tale here about exactly what the title says. A wonderful female voice sings wordless vocals a la PF's "The Great Gig in the Sky" for the part of the Siren. The guitar solo has a swirling effect, perhaps a Uni-Vibe pedal. Another truly wonderful song.Track 7 - Enigmatic Terminus (3:58)After a synth tone, it sounds like a string quartet. Then when the band kicks in, the music takes a turn for the spooky. There are some interesting chord progressions here. The main lyric theme is "Driving to Distruction". Every song on this album, thus far, has really drawn me in. I feel like I have entered a world all of its own.Track 8 - Legend of Mary Jo (14:14)While all of the preceding tracks have been in the 3-5 minute range, this closing epic clocks in at over 14. Let's see where this journey takes us. The opening line "My name is Mary Jo" is already intriguing, as it is being sung by a male! We are in 6-8 here. Phideaux demonstrates some falsetto notes here. Mary Jo is prophesying about events in 2062 when we hit the second verse. The meter has been alternating between 4-4 and 6-8. There is a nice guitar solo around 2:30. There are some odd-meter shifts happening in this instrumental break. Wordless female vocals join the soundscape. I'm not sure who Amy is, but she leads the battalion. At 5 minutes there is a double time section with honky-tonk piano, joined by harmonized guitars. There are some cool, Chicago-like horn parts interspersed. There are many dynamic and mood changes as this song progresses. There is a sax solo as we cross the 9 minute mark. Things slow down and get mysterious around 9:40. There are overlapping spoken words after 10 minutes. Then BANG at 10:22, there is a very Yes-like bass and drum explosion, leading to the most overtly prog part of the album. There is a lot going on here, in the best possible way! The Chris Squire style bass part is simply stunning! At around 12:30, the opening line returns, but in a very different setting. This track is more than just a song, it is an experience! Incredible, instant classic epic, unlike anything I have heard before.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:WOW! This album simply must be heard by anyone who appreciates artistically presented well-produced and well-written songs. I really need to go back and dig into Phideaux's back catalog much deeper if this album is indicative of his style. I was leaning toward a 4.5 rating, until Legend of Mary Jo took it into the next level. 4.75 stars or 95%. The race for best prog album of 2026 just got even more difficult to decide!

items.body: Review by maxsmusic — It's hard to describe this band without using the word symphonic. They truly know how to make a track that delves into very thick realms of lush synthesized motifs with flutes and guitars. They may have never achieved commercial success like the other progressive power houses of the 70's, but they influenced so many bands that took their musical ideas and went into paths that resulted in bands such as Opeth, Marillion and Spock's Beard. Camel is like a well oiled machine that could churn out melodic music in abundance. This retrospective is the gold at the end of rainbow, and it covers their catalogue in their glory years. No other band could combine lyrics, beautiful melodies and harmonies like this group. They were tragically overlooked because they were never flashy, grandiose or otherwise extroverted. They just wrote consistent music that conveys emotional beauty. 4.5 stars

items.excerpt: Review by fernandootero28 — Why Drama Is One of Yes's Greatest AlbumsThe earlier Yes albums always struck me as demanding; Drama, on the other hand, felt downright intimidating.I first discovered Drama roughly thirteen years after its release. Like much of Yes's catalog, I didn't encounter it in real time but retrospectively, in the early 1990s. At the time, I had a very specific goal: I was a student determined to study the bass and keyboard parts throughout the band's entire discography.
items.body: Review by fernandootero28 — Why Drama Is One of Yes's Greatest AlbumsThe earlier Yes albums always struck me as demanding; Drama, on the other hand, felt downright intimidating.I first discovered Drama roughly thirteen years after its release. Like much of Yes's catalog, I didn't encounter it in real time but retrospectively, in the early 1990s. At the time, I had a very specific goal: I was a student determined to study the bass and keyboard parts throughout the band's entire discography. Yes was my daily study material, and I was an obsessive admirer of their music.That context probably shaped my relationship with Drama forever. I didn't come to the album carrying the controversies that surrounded its release or the debates about lineup changes. I came to it as a musician?with pencil, paper, headphones, and the desire to understand what they were playing.What immediately struck me was the level of execution placed entirely in the service of creating a collection of works of remarkable beauty and artistic stature.I found myself listening over and over again to Chris Squire's and Geoff Downes' lines, trying to understand what was happening and to play along with the album.From the very first day, I experienced it as an extraordinary display of composition, performance, and artistic ambition.It seemed reasonable to me that Chris Squire, Steve Howe, and Alan White?three of the principal architects of the Yes sound?would not have jeopardized the artistic stature of the band. If Trevor Horn and Geoff Downes were there, nobody was in a better position to make that decision than they were."Into the Lens" deserves a chapter of its own.The piece opens with one of the most impressive introductions in the entire Yes catalog. The level of ensemble precision is remarkable. The perfectly synchronized 32nd-note passages and the polyrhythms are astonishing. I still remember my amazement at the collective precision with which the musicians sustain such complexity simultaneously.Adding to that is a particularly innovative harmonic language in the introduction, where Steve Howe develops melodic lines that expand the band's traditional vocabulary without losing its identity. The result is a work of enormous technical complexity that never sacrifices beauty or musical direction.And then there is "Tempus Fugit."If there is one song that encapsulates the spirit of Drama, it is probably this one.It is an example of progressive rock in which the rock element feels more powerful than ever. The energy is ferocious, yet that aggression coexists with some of the most extreme technical challenges in Yes's entire career. What is extraordinary is that none of those difficulties seem to exist for the sake of displaying virtuosity. Everything serves the musical impulse of the piece.Hearing the count-off and imagining what it would mean to occupy any one of those four instrumental chairs onstage is dizzying. Playing this music with the precision, energy, and intensity that Drama demands requires a remarkably well-regulated nervous system.In "Run Through the Light," I hear one of Trevor Horn's strongest performances on the album. From "Machine Messiah" onward, it was already clear to me that Horn was not simply replacing Jon Anderson. He was something far more legitimate: a Yes singer.Horn belonged to a generation that had grown up listening to the band. By the time he joined, the musical language of Yes was already part of his artistic education. He appears not as an outsider attempting to fill an empty seat, but as someone who had absorbed the band's musical culture for years and understood its vocabulary deeply.Chris Squire, meanwhile, draws on stylistic devices that recall some of his most recognizable creative trademarks. Certain figures immediately evoke the logic of "Heart of the Sunrise": rhythmic patterns and ostinatos that are unmistakably part of his language. Yet this is not nostalgia. It is style.Geoff Downes navigates that grammar by doubling many of those figures on piano and keyboards. Executing this material with such precision is a considerable technical challenge in itself. Downes brings both his own musical personality and the technical command necessary to integrate naturally into what feels like a finely engineered mechanism.I have always found it curious that we believe we can put someone else's silence into words. Yet, playing that game for a moment, I have always had the feeling that Steve Howe, Chris Squire, and Alan White arrived at Drama determined to reach the highest level of technical and expressive achievement they were capable of attaining, even surpassing what they had accomplished on extraordinary albums such as Relayer.Not in an effort to surpass anyone else, but to surpass themselves. Something akin to what Genesis achieved on A Trick of the Tail.And Geoff Downes fits perfectly into that pursuit, bringing harmonic imagination and technical ability that allow him to occupy his place naturally within an exceptionally sophisticated musical machine.If Howe, Squire, and White set out to push virtuosity to its limits while placing it entirely in the service of beauty and artistic depth, they unquestionably succeeded.Perhaps that is why Drama remains such a unique album within the Yes discography.What I hear is five musicians operating simultaneously at one of the highest levels of concentration, precision, and risk.fernando otero

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Although it was the same band as on the previous album, the music was different, and Jethro Tull opened many doors with Benefit. Stand Up was luminous, and while it sounded British...it was like Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer's London subsidiary, with an American touch, a hint of Woodstock. Ian Anderson changed his singing style, modulating better and abandoning his blues roots, and John Evan joined the band in the recording studio. "With You There to Help Me" already shows classical influences, as well as flamenco, but maintaining that raw rock, that dirty guitar sound that made Tull dangerous in the 60s.With a hard rock undertone at the beginning that could have been Black Sabbath, Anderson sings on "Nothing to Say" using modal scales, typical of medieval religious choral music. It's here that the change begins, in the composition, and continues in the performance, without abandoning the freshness that characterized the band in its early days... however, one doesn't imagine a jazzy/bluesy improvisation here as in their beginnings. The transition towards the strong progressive period and the Thick as a Brick era had begun, leaving behind great albums like this one and Aqualung."Alive and Well and Living In" is an example of how, in 2:44 minutes, a compendium of everything can be contained: the emerging 60s and the nascent 70s, the dreamy pop ballad, rock, epic music, there's even a piano solo, courtesy of John Evan, the first of those duets with Ian's flute that would later become more frequent."Son" shows us that compositional mastery that was already beginning to emerge, weaving together very disparate parts with an invisible thread, which would culminate in the long epics of the future... Ian singing like never before, and Martin Barre revealing himself as the ideal partner."For Michael Collins, Jeffrey and Me" are those great hippie songs (of which they wouldn't have many) and with Ian competing for the position of best symphonic singer with Greg Lake."To Cry You a Song" is possibly the first adaptation of J.S. Bach's style of counterpoint, but transposed here to the electric guitar, creating a "Baroque Fugue" framework. Ian also plays guitar alongside Martin. Including an improvised section in the middle that gives a live session feel, the rhythm section of Glenn Cornick on bass and Clive Bunker on drums adapted quite well to the emerging complexity of the music; they came from the previous period and would remain until the next album as long as the transition lasted."Inside" seems like the best example of the missing link between Stand Up and Benefit; that British pop that was produced during this era will never lose its charm. With the two Jethro Tulls coexisting, the one from the past and the one from the future, we arrive at that present of 1970 where Play in Time leaves us for posterity the psychedelic experiment with reversed tapes, echoes and various effects that together with the flute are the final touch along with "Sossity: You're a Woman", the serene ballad that is among the most beautiful of this period, showing Barre's acoustic guitar facet as well as once again Ian's successful voice, which unite masterful grandiloquence...with simple intimacy.

items.body: Review by Soul2Create — Yes is back with Aurora!, their third album in five years, not counting other efforts like Arc of life, Xeno-x-Xeno, DBA or even Jon Anderson and the Geeks (all of them great, no distinctions here). We are having plently of new Yes or Yes-styled music to hear and its surprising this is happening when the band is approaching its 60th anniversary. So, The Quest, Mirror to the sky and Aurora are supposed to function like a trilogy in sound and soul, let's see what Aurora brings to the table:Aurora - title track and honestly one of the best songs they have composed in their careers. It has everything to love for a fan, the bass, the keyboards, the guitar, the voice, even the orchestra is very well included. Maybe, just maybe, the beginning is too Disneysh, but anyway is a top song (9.5/10)Turnaround situation - I am supposed to like this one more. Again it has all of the ingredients I like in a Yes song, but this time it does not click for me, maybe is too poppy for my taste. I love the instrumental breaks and the ending though (6.5/10)Love Lies Dreaming - almost merging with the ending of the previous track, this one is built over a catchy melody, I like the second half of the song a lot, with the chorus interchanged with Howe's guitar solos (8.75/10)Countermovement - The epic. Howe's guitar leads everything here, from the complex start, to the melodic middle sections including country, pop, psychedelic rock (...that Wurm feeling again...) and keyboard-guitar solo fights, to the emotional finale. An effective pastiche indeed! (8.5/10)Ariadne - classic orchestral opening to support Davison. The overall feeling is a bit OST-like, BUT, the song shifts in the middle to a Conspiracy/Squire inpired theme led by Sherwood that is one of my favourite moments of the album. Good track! (8/10)All Hands on Deck - distorted guitar it is! a bit repetitive but the chorus is infectious and I absolutely dig those keyboards, almost funky! Really fun song (9/10)Outside the Box - as it name suggest, is an experimental track, based on voice multitracks and keybeaord effects (6/10) Emotional Intelligence - a pop song to close the album. Again, Howe shines with its guitar (5.5/10).Jambustin - First bonus track, some psychedelic pop mixed with funky grooves (6/10)Watching the River Roll - classic rock vibes here. Good track, awesome keyboards! (7.5/10)Overall, I agree with some reviews that claim this to be the best album of the three last ones. It is the most consistent, although it does not reach the heights of Mirror to the sky. If I were to do a ranking with this line-up where Downes-Howe are the core members of Yes, it would be Drama-Aurora-Fly from here-The Quest-Mirror to the sky, being the title track of the last one the best of all.Four stars, recommended for any prog lover, and a must if you are a Yes fan! So happy to see one of my favourite bands alive and well.

items.body: Review by EduardoV_RJ — Van der Graaf Generator functions as a sort of "Anti-Genesis" within Progressive Rock. This is not a statement about quality, but rather style. While the symphonic prog movement drew its main inspiration from Romantic or Baroque classical music, another current drank deeply from jazz and contemporary classical music. This is precisely the case with Van der Graaf Generator.It is easy to perceive the use of minimalism in more experimental bands like Magma or Univers Z�ro, but within VdGG, this device takes on a different dynamic. Instead of running in circles, they move in a spiral, building progressive layers on top of the same theme until reaching a climax. The music is claustrophobic, yet no less theatrical. The lyrics tackle modern personal struggles, such as the masks we wear in society or the inner world of the songwriter, who converses more with his guitar than with human beings. Make no mistake: this is not classical music, it is rock. They never allow sophistication to eliminate the genre's raw essence.This work marks the farewell of the band's classic lineup, but it is by no means a minor album. The overall quality of the tracks is excellent, highlighted by "A Place to Survive" (featuring an impressive climax), the epic "Meurglys III"?whose title references vocalist Peter Hammill's guitar?and the dense "Masks."Ultimately, World Record is not just the final testament of Van der Graaf Generator's classic lineup, but proof that progressive rock can be urgent, sharp, and dangerous. The genre's clich�s often evoke images of long instrumental suites, excessive keyboards, and constant shifts in mood. This record shatters that stereotype, proving that there is far more diversity and rawness in Progressive Rock than common knowledge assumes.

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — And now we have finally arrived at the end (for now) of my journey through Rock Progressivo Italiano. And what better way to end such a phenomenal ride with a review of one of my favorite records of all time, Palepoli, by Osanna. Everything about this album is absolutely one hundred percent perfect in my eyes. If I had to pick one album that truly represents my music taste as a whole, it could very well be this one. It definitely takes the cake for my number one album from Italy, and could legitimately be a contender of my number one album to ever exist. Everything from the musicianship, pacing, artwork, concept, and everything in between is just incredible, and to this day my most prized possession is an original 1973 copy of the vinyl. The fusion of just gorgeous folk music, trippy and heavy jams, intricately woven progressive rock, and jazzy freak outs makes for one of the best musical experiences of my life whenever I listen to it. And every member of the band executes it in the best way possible, never missing a beat or losing my interest. Speaking of the band members, allow me to highlight them really quickly. We have one of my personal heroes, Lino Vairetti, taking care the vocals (which are some the greatest and most powerful I've ever heard), rhythm guitar, mellotron, and the ARP 2600 synthesizer, Danilo Rustici taking of all other guitars, electric piano, vox organ, and backing vocals, Elio D'Anna playing both tenor and soprano saxophone, as well as flute and backing vocals, Lello Brandi on bass, and Massimo Guarino drumming as well doing the percussion. As a drummer, I'm ecstatic to say that Massimo's drumming on this record influenced me a lot and I absolutely love how he plays on this thing. I wonder if Lino and the lads knew that they were recording what could be (for me) the greatest studio album of all time in that studio in Naples, surrounded by the pure beauty of the city and its nature.�The album consists of two flawless twenty-minute suites, with a reprise/interlude being the only interruption, and no other format for such a grand and vibrant record could've encapsulated it better than this. In the beginning of the first song, Oro Caldo, we are on this dreamy, acoustic-based piece with minimal percussion, guitars, and flutes, backed by the chants and sounds of the early morning of the Mediterranean. It feels like pure bliss the way the band floats you along this musical sunrise right before the energy of the real day begins. And that energy comes around two minutes into the piece, where, out of nowhere, we get this rush of bombastic and pounding rhythms backed by the upbeat nature of everything as it dashes by you. Cheerful cries can be heard as solos fly over you, before time seems to stop and we're transported into this fog of various echoes and mysterious noises. I love how the band plays with your mind like this, throwing you in and out of chaos, leaving you confused and eager as to what will happen next in the best way possible. The haze slowly grows as the music finally begins to settle like sand coming back to the ocean floor so gently you barely notice it. Everything is crafted so astonishingly well that the real world seems to change itself to go with the darkened mood of the music. Very slowly, the clouds begin to clear and are finally broken by this absolutely stunning chord progression on the mellotron. But before long, these menacing and tribal rhythms start back up, revving up faster and faster as all of this drive of power builds up further and further in such a short amount of time, only being interrupted by brief yet exquisite moments of heavenly melodies, only to launch you back into the lunacy of everything, with wailing saxophones, screeching guitars, and sporadic and manic-sounding blasts from the drums, all being wrapped up by the band cutting all of this electric madness off and into the soothing strums of an acoustic guitar and mellow atmosphere of this magical world the band has put on to wax. The ending is this sinister yet almost carnival-sounding rhythm with uncanny energy that seems to allow the band to fill in monstrous improvisations, making this schizophrenic-like tone. The last of side one is simply a refrain of the opening Oro Caldo titled Stanza Citt�, with the only difference being strange and cryptic sounds that have been spliced in between the various moments. And that wraps up the first half of this masterpiece. Unforgettable and absolutely incredible!�Side two contains the longest track at over twenty minutes long, and with the title of Animale Senza Respiro, it's another one of my favourite compositions of all time. The record explodes in the opening with this crushing, brutal composition that the band drones on, pounding it over and over again with minimal changes, before almost instantly coming to a stop and going into this ambient dread that fills the room with a hazy, more natural sound. As the music grows and gets louder, eventually the band joins back in and goes into more heavy rock music, bouncing between jazz fusion and trippy, carefully assembled progressive rock. I love how the band flawlessly meanders through the piece and makes everything feel so natural and yet retain an uncanny value in the music itself. Eventually, the band falls back into this dreadful atmosphere of background instrumentation fusing together to make a singular backing noise, only pierced by these absolutely beautiful acoustic guitars and Lino's voice, acting as a force of good in this monstrous composition. It's a nice break that fits in amazingly with the other moments of this track, despite feeling so different. Soon enough, it's consumed by this aura, and we're only left with questions as the band leaves on this dreamy landscape of darkening clouds, which is eventually broken by a small light of acapella, piercing the storm and bringing the listener a glimmer of hope. It grows and grows before finally breaking back into the gloomy, yet rocking sound that continues to expand with a more painful angle of the music here, and eventually, right as the band gets to its peak, they cut the music's throat, and the tension goes out again. It's like they're edging us to the grand finale, and they know it. They're taking their time, and I love them for that. In the last few minutes of the song, they go into these insane refrains of other sections of the song, bringing back all the best moments from the song and adding to the chaos of intensity that's been building up for nearly twenty minutes by this point. Eventually, after a wild and complicated drum solo, we get the final refrain, which is of the opening movement with vocals added on, showing the final form of the musical adventure that was this piece. However, there is one more chapter that closes this masterpiece. A slow, brooding rhythm that goes slowly with a dark vibe that the band lets control the entire mood of the music and the listener, before growing into one, last, grand crescendo that closes this album as a grand finale.�In conclusion, I want you to take a wild guess, based on what I just wrote up there, about what I think of this record. Yes, this is indeed a musical essential. Everything I love about music is packed into these forty minutes of perfection, and the band could not have made it any better. The absolute pinnacle of Rock Progressivo Italiano and (in my opinion) one of the peaks of music as a whole. I cannot say it enough, I adore this record, and there is close to nothing better than it. Palepoli is an astounding and well-deserved perfect, 5/5. Thank you, Osanna, for your contribution to my life and musical history!

items.body: Review by alainPP — Tollheit is the musical project of composer-keyboardist Robert Doucette. 2024 sees the introduction of AI-generated vocals'good, bad, let's see on this short album."Maze of Delirium" opens with a symphonic sound built on velvety, catchy keyboards and a playful melody reminiscent of the '80s and '90s. "Sick Minds Think Alike" is a typical AOR track that could get radio airplay if the world were a better place. The AI ​​vocals can be a hindrance, but that's intentional; the track, with its fat synth reminiscent of Genesis's baby, and the very synthetic drums, is jarring, which is a shame because the track itself is quite charismatic. "Venal Clowns Died at a Ruse Dinner" has a juicy, melodic, and solemn intro. A mainstream rock track plays in the background, reminiscent of the '80s, with the saxophone amplifying this effect. The vocals, which I've already heard sampled elsewhere, are a hindrance; I feel betrayed in a way. The symphonic arrangement becomes laudatory, inviting progressive reverie. "Spilled Milk on the Joker's Table" provides a welcome interlude, bolstered by prog-metal rhythms and the Genesis-esque keyboard of "Burning Ropes"; another catchy track, inviting you to float among the clouds. A masterful launch of "Rotten Fruits of Labor" unfolds with the sinister feel of a horror film; the synth reprises the same melody, and the track oscillates between AI vocals, repetitive drums, and a familiar tune. The embellishing synth and guitar solo amplify the track's quality, though they become somewhat repetitive. "Sell Nicole of Earth" follows, illuminated by a thousand lights with the synth swirling in the air over a well-paced symphonic suite. The multi-layered arrangement confirms Robert's assiduous mastery at the controls. "Garden of Eden" and its solemn intro plunge the listener into the musical journey. The female voice, beautiful but unreal, calls out to me; I feel betrayed. Wouldn't her voice, or that of a singer friend, have been more suitable? My memory searches for the owner of those strings, distracting me from the otherwise simple, melodic piece.Tollheit, meaning madness in German, is likely to disorient you. This is entirely fabricated progressive rock, falling flat after their masterful previous album.

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. Formentera Lady begins, a classic jazzy jam with ethereal vocals and a latent, unrestrained saxophone for the slow, swirling build-up; Raymond is the new voice, reminiscent of another band, with soprano Paulina backing him up; the finale, with its wild, flowing saxophone, feels a bit underwhelming for this king in pre-hibernation, even disappointing.2. Sailor's Tale is still jazzy, but with frenetic guitar and saxophone, giving you goosebumps. The crimson sound returns in experimental mode, a make-or-break moment; Robert adds his Frippian touch with sharp, razor-sharp riffs softened by the Mellotron?in fact, he does everything here; a progressive crescendo where the rhythm is captivating, with the drums again prominent, here featuring newcomer Ian playing King Crimson; the final build-up is intended to be epic and repetitive with a drone, already present back then, vibrant and... long. 3. "The Letters" finally delivers the signature sound: a melancholic vocal over a crystalline arpeggio; the saxophone cuts through everything, aggressive, reminiscent of a Manu Dibango in full flow. Mel might overdo it a bit, as he tempers his breath, restoring the necessary progression. The problem is that these sounds lack cohesion and stand out, sounding more like a session recording than a fully formed track. It's a shame because the flute has a strong prog vibe, but it's not quite there yet.4. "Ladies of the Road" is about groupies. This text is particularly relevant today given current events, which explains my delayed review. It explores the temptation of having slept with an artist and the potential rejection years later. The vocals are worthy of Albion, with a choir reminiscent of the Beatles, and the jazzy-bluesy atmosphere lacks guitar, with the saxophone being predominant. Robert finally unleashes the energy of despair in the solo, hinting at the austere, muted, and haunting cruelty of the future 'Red'; in short, avant-garde might be synonymous with a damp squib.5. Prelude: Song of the Gulls, a neo-classical instrumental piece, features string instruments reminiscent of the era of French kings, as if Robert were envisioning himself with a crown; a fine exercise, ultimately more accessible than the other elaborate noise-based tracks.6. Islands, the eponymous piece, is long and invites hope; a solemn piano, a Crimson-esque voice, and a grandiloquent, delicate, neo-classical melody; a beautiful detour with the emotive trumpet, a minimalist variation that unfortunately lacks intensity, a sound that is post-rock before its time.A silence, then the outro with pre-show chatter and tuning, just enough to stretch the album past 40 minutes?

items.body: Review by SilverLight59 — This is a band that doesn't seem to get nearly enough love. They have quietly put out three classy albums, and now a fourth, with seemingly modest attention, and relatively few reviews. So, let's see what we can do about that.I have been following 35 Tapes from their first album, and I have to say that I like them more with each release. This, their newest effort, "Veil On Life", continues the upward arc with good style. Does anything bad come out of Norway in the realm of progressive music? I venture to say, not so much. And this is no exception! The band's web site has reviews that describe their sound as 'random' symphonic rock along with delicate passages, beautiful vocals and explosive instrumentals, a warm open sound that can easily invite the listener on a symphonic and cinematic journey through moods, space, and time. At times evoking the symphonic grandeur of the early prog foundation stones, however, the group also touches on the melancholy art rock of more modern artists as well. Another review stated the following, 35 tapes provide crescendos that can blow your socks off; however, the magic lies not in showy pyrotechnics or dazzling virtuosity. Instead, every talented musician in the group joins into a harmonious union to channel various moods. It is easy to agree with these assessments as each song takes the listener on a focused, yet meandering journey that is most enjoyable. There are many occasions when one thinks a song is ending and it wanders into an entirely different phase, yet it all ties together. Part of what ties it all together is the strong choruses that tend to make the pieces more accessible than they might otherwise be. That's not to say that there aren't some powerful chords here and there, and sometimes there are sections where there are build ups that seem to be on the verge of totally breaking loose, but there is always a controlled restraint.Summing it up, the band itself, giving insight of their approach, says, the "35 Tapes philosophy is "Not too many notes, but the right ones; not fixed chords, but floating, open chords; not virtuoso, but true." This self-assessment, indeed, accurately describes their approach to what they give us. There are plenty of moments where a particular instrument will weave in and out of sections of a song, grabbing your attention, but not overwhelming. As the song moves on, you anticipate its return, which sometimes it does, and sometimes it doesn't. This unpredictability keeps things fresh and interesting. If you are looking for references for the influences to be found, you might look for ones such as Genesis, King Crimson, Yes, David Sylvan , Talk Talk - in their more avant-guard period, RPWL, Phideaux, airbag, maybe even a hint of Bowie here and there, and of course Pink Floyd. One has to ask, has anyone not been influenced by Pink Floyd?So, some brief thoughts on the album itself. The artwork for the album cover is their most dramatic so far, nice colors, and continuing the circle theme that is now on three of the four albums. The figure at the end of the tunnel suggests that something new is in the works, and so it proves to be as the overall feel of the set of songs is a bit more firm and powerful, yet their established wanderings are not altogether lost.The length of the album follows their established pattern of about 40-45 minutes, which works well. So it's about the length of an old fashioned LP. Remember those? With just six tracks, the songs are all a moderate length which provides ample opportunity for them to develop, evolve, and unwind. Even after multiple listens you will find that there are new subtle nuances to be found. The songs are few, but the quality is very high. It leaves you wanting more. I suppose that is what their back catalogue is for. So, on to the tracks.Hallway (6:43) So, this opener starts with some strong guitar work and synths lying underneath. Vocals come quickly, leading to some very nice soft lyrical sections, the pace and strength of the track undulating between a controlled intensity and contrasting softness. At about the half way point, drops way off for a piano interlude, and begins rising again with a very pleasant vocal section, low synths and plucking guitar notes until full band is resurrected for the last minute or so for a very nice instrumental finish. Nice start! (8.5/10) Waters (5:14) This track also opens with some big guitar chords, and synths cradling the forward momentum, building, building, and the drop off to move into the vocals. The lyrics here are clever and thought provoking, contrasting the weak from the strong, the privileged from the lowly, and where did we all come from? Lots of big isolated chords creating a sonic tapestry. While the guitars are prominent, the synths have a bigger roll in this track, and create much of the energy here moving to the finish. Another strong track. (8.5/10)Brise' Vole' (7:41) In classical ballet, "bris� vol�" translates to "flying bris�" or "flying broken step". It is a dynamic, jumping step where a dancer alternates between beating their legs in the air (a bris�) and landing cleanly on a single leg, often traveling diagonally across the stage. This then, sets the context for this track, a cinematic, operatic, piece that lyrically encourages self-examination. It begins against whimsical piano and keys, very ballad oriented, then elevates to a fuller level with a crying guitar, restrained, not excessive but moving. About 2:50 in the guitar works get much bolder, pace and volume of the track intensifying. Nice instrumental section follows, reworking the themes, building up again. The keys pushing underneath. Nice! Last minute and a half reopen the whimsical opening theme and vocals and gradually fades out. My favorite track this time around! (9.5/10)Borrowed Time (6:24) Softer guitar start this time, has a bit of a Yes vibe through the underlying synths, but powers up quickly with solid base lines, more powerful drumming, and up front lead guitar. At 3:30 drops off into a contemplative instrumental interlude, followed by another gradual build up with vocals. Some pretty intense lead guitar to close out. The most power oriented track on this album, but probably also the least multidimensional. Still, not bad. (8/10)Clueless (6:07) Opens with a simple acoustic guitar strum, bursts forward with nice electric guitar over the top, engaging vocals, very pleasant, very accessible. As close to pop as this band may ever get. About midway, keeps growing in intensity and then drops off to a synth soundscape, not pop anymore, but still accessible. And then the final build up to the ending, guitar work is very enjoyable. Not particularly complex for 35 Tapes, but a real earworm type of track that you will like coming back to. (8.5/10)Cities (8:23) Starts big again like the first and second track, a mid-tempo pace. Drops down to a slower sound scape and vocals, nice synth section follows. Kind of jazzy at points. The full band is being highlighted here with all the instruments creating a big sound, but still notably restrained. The keys play a forward role, and then suddenly at about 5:20 big sonic guitar bursts it way to the forefront and just as suddenly ends. Song over? No. it comes roaring back, and rolls in to a vocal section, and then final powerful close out with full band playing forcefully closing out the track and the album with a sense of finality. (9.5/10)In conclusion, all in all, a very strong effort! While previous albums tended to be a bit more atmospheric, and meandering, these songs, while having those elements, seem a bit tighter and more structured. There is also a bit more intensity as the guitar work is more up front and center, although there is still plenty of keys and synths. Perhaps this time the synths are overall a bit more restrained, although they clearly have some shining and lead moments. Lastly, the vocals deserve some earnest recognition. This can be a weakness with many prog bands, but not here. This is my first review in quite a while, but one I thought would be worth doing. Definitely would like this band to get more attention and a wider audience. We'll give this one a solid four-star rating. Cheers!

items.body: Review by andrea — "Vacuum" is the second studio album by The Watch and was released in 2004 on the independent Lizard Music label with a renewed line up featuring Simone Rossetti (vocals, flute, tambou), Roberto Leoni (drums, percussion), Gabriele Manzini (keyboards, synthesizers), Ettore Salati (guitars), Sergio Taglioni (piano, organ, Moog, Mellotron, synthesizers) and Marco Schembri (bass, guitars). Genesis from the early seventies are still the main source of inspiration and the band demonstrates not only to have studied their style in depth but to have absorbed it and, in some ways, made it their own...The opener, "Hills", is just a short introduction that depicts a mysterious, peaceful place in the dark surrounded by distant traffic lights. All around little shining cars seem dancing like dolphins in the sea. It's a secret time...Then, in "Damage Mode" the music and lyrics evoke a young man recalling a youthful trauma. He can't deny the anger and hatred toward the man who caused it. In his mind, he sees the images of a film where the female protagonist is ready to run to escape the attack of a lion that wants to devour her..."Wonderland" paints a beautiful city full of lights and signs. It's a world that invites you to spend your money with the illusion of achieving happiness through parties and slot machines, easy women and alcohol. But all this is just an illusion and isn't enough to hide the inner emptiness of those who allow themselves to be seduced by the sirens of a merciless consumerism..."Shining Bald Heads" describes a strange character, someone who appears like a rainbow when your day seems over: Mr. Doubt. During the day, his bald head shines in the suburbs and outlying neighbourhoods, but when the workday ends he reappears with his claws planted in your dreams. He's a sign of life and sometimes it would be better to heed his friendly advice..."Out Of The Land" tells of the solitude and peace one can experience in a small town far from the hectic life of big cities, and of the strange and contradictory feelings experienced by those who leave the chaos of a metropolis to take refuge in the tranquillity of a distant and all-too-silent place..."Goddess" depicts the image of a man singing the praises of his beloved, a woman who for him is a true goddess to be adored and loved blindly and unconditionally, and without whom his life risks losing all meaning..."Deeper Still" is a lullaby for a child born on a cold winter morning. White snow falls on the newborn troubled life while his future is taking form. The parents sense a kind of passing of the baton in the relay race of life. The prevailing feeling is small and fragile: it's simply love...The long, complex title track, "The Vacuum", is a suite divided into five parts that was inspired by the character of Serge Abrahamovitch Voronoff Voronoff, a French surgeon of Russian origin working in the 1920s and 1930s best known for his practice of transplantation of living cells, tissues and organs from animals monkeys to men to increase sexual power and as an anti-ageing therapy. The piece opens with the excerpt from the report of a patrol of the French Gendarmerie. A strange creature was seen running outside Voronff's castle, near the border with the Italian town of Ventimiglia. The piece continues with excerpts from Voronoff's diary, which address the ethical implications of the scientist's work. The third part is a surreal exposition of the creature's sensations. The fourth part contains a warning about the excesses of experimentation: those who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones! The fifth and final part features the creature's discovery in a pool of dreams...On the whole, a very good work in pure Genesis style!

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — It turns out, I accidentally did my calculations wrong and did one less review than I was supposed to. I wanted to post my final review of the Grand Rock Progressivo Italiano scene on my last day of school to cap off this year in high school, but I'm one day off, so I'll be posting this to clear that gap. For me, this is the last great Osanna album to ever come out. Sure, Sundance is okay, and the modern records they've been putting out are also alright, but this is the last one to have that more complex and vintage sound of classic Osanna. It seems like ProgArchives agrees with my statement, seeing how this was the last album Osanna released to obtain over a hundred ratings (as of writing this), and it is also one of the last albums they made to have more than a 3.5/5 rating in the band's discography, although Prog Family also has the same rating as it (again, as of writing this review). When looking at the personnel, the lineup includes Lino Vairetti on lead vocals along with various guitars and keyboards, Danilo Rustici on the rest of the guitars and keyboards along with the lead vocals on a singular track (Promised Land), Elio d'Anna on saxophone and flute, Lello Brandi on bass and effects, Massimo Guarino on drums and percussion, and two guest musicians named Corrado Rustici and Enzo Vallicelli who do guitar work and percussion respectively. So before I even get into the music, the cover art for this album might possibly be one of my favorite album covers by Osanna, with the captivating image of a deconstructed whale floating in space being really eye-catching and unique, and the fact that it was made entirely by their drummer, Massimo, is even cooler. When looking at the music on it, this record has a lot more English vocals than Italian vocals, and I know the band already experimented with English lyrics on L'Uomo, but here they are a lot more relevant and overall weaker. The one song that is sung in Italian, Il Castello Dell'es, is just fantastic and is easily one of the best songs ever released by Osanna. The title track is also magnificent and feels very grand and emotional compared to the normal heavy rock of Osanna. While those two are my favorite compositions off of the album, the rest of the tracks on here are still quite good, and each has its own unique and distinct feel. Two Boys is more hard rock, Promised Land has a more simple and emotional touch, and the closer of Somehow, Somewhere, Sometime is a return to the band's normal progressive rock energy. In conclusion, while it may have not been quite as good as the album that came before it (Palepoli), Osanna's Landscape of Life is still a great album with excellent arrangements and depth not only in the actual songs but also in the deeply touching moments. Therefore, my final rating would be a very strong 4/5, and it is just barely out of reach of a low 4.25/5.

items.body: Beth Willer   Voices of Ascension: Canticle of the Sun Voices of Ascension, Beth Willer, conductor Church of the Ascension May 21, 2026 Published in Sequenza 21 By Christian Carey   NEW YORK – Beth Willer, Director of Choral Activities at Peabody Conservatory and Artistic Director of Lorelei Ensemble, served as guest conductor for Voices of Ascension’s recent Canticle of the Sun concert. To say the program was ambitious is to undersell the challenges posed by all of the pieces. Most choral ensembles, even professional ensembles, would consider any one of these works to be an inclusion sufficient to prove their capabilities as interpreters of recent music, and move on to the rest of the evening. Voices of Ascension and Willer had other ideas. Ellen Reid’s Oscillations: 100 Years and Forever, for chorus and percussion, opened the program. Percussionists Clara Warnaar and Colleen Bernstein were called upon to inhabit a number of roles – no pun intended. During the course of the piece, thrumming drumming and dulcet textures from pitched percussion supported singing from the chorus and four soloists that moved similarly through a wide dynamic range. The piece’s text deals with the cycles of nature operating over the course of a century in Los Angeles, and the varieties of repetition suggested by the title appeared in asymmetric waves of activity. All My Salt Runs Short, settings of three texts by the New Zealand poet Chris Holdoway and twentieth century Venezuelan writer Miguel Otero Silva by composer Celeste Oram, was given its premiere by Ascension, joined by organist Paolo Bordignon. The piece takes its title from a phrase in the poem by Silva, and the juxtaposition of salt found in oceans and tears was a moving throughline in the work. The relationship between chorus and organ was interesting, and showed the trust the composer had in the singers, as long stretches of a cappella singing were followed by passages that then synced up with the organ. These were rendered with impressive tuning, with fetching added note and chromatic harmonies creating a shimmering texture. Like Oscillations, groups of soloists and different divisi afforded the possibilities of multiple strands of activity, and the aforementioned chordal events were matched by supple, interweaving lines. As with the other programmed pieces, All My Salt Runs Short features percussion, here instruments of an atmospheric variety, a rain stick, wind wand, and whirly tube. As the work neared its conclusion, the organ was turned off with a cluster chord still depressed, causing it to dip down and fade away, leaving the choir to conclude with a held, haunting echo. Willer brought out numerous subtleties in this quite detailed score, eliciting an affecting performance. Olivier Messiaen didn’t write much choral music, but Clytus Gottwald’s arrangement of Louange á L’Éternité de Jésus, a movement from Le Quatuor pour la fins du Temps, using a text by the composer, worked well. Organist John Gillock gave a rafter shaking rendition of Messiaen’s Apparition de l’église éternelle that demonstrated the plenitude of colorful registrations that Ascension’s pipe organ affords. The title piece of the concert, for the unusual scoring of solo cello, percussion, and chorus, was Sofia Gubaidulina’s Canticle of the Sun (1997). An animated performance that in places took on a ritualistic demeanor, it was given a powerful rendition. Solo cellist Tommy Mesa was required to play abundantly virtuosic passages, including finely tuned, wide ranging glissandos, which were impressively rendered. About midway through, another set of challenges for Mesa presented themselves. Scordatura, retuning of strings to different pitches, occurred on the fly, and eventually his cello was left behind altogether in favor of percussion instruments, which culminated in Mesa on a suspended cymbal, in clangorous crashes, in the middle of the hall. After this climax, gradually equilibrium was restored, Mesa returning to the stage, and his instrument, playing the key glissando gestures of the piece to close. Throughout, the choir alternated between accompanying and engaging in dialogue with the soloist and the percussionist cohort. There was much to admire about Voices of Ascension’s performance. They are in excellent hands with their director, Dennis Keene, but Willer’s conducting and curation make one hope she will join them again to make similarly inspired music.   The post Voices of Ascension: Canticle of the Sun appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: During the Ottoman and, later, British occupation of Palestine, Palestinian women developed the mlolah to pass messages through prison walls: a vocal technique that disguises meaning by inserting “la” syllables throughout the lyrics, converting what sounds like a love song into a carrier of news, plans, and coded solidarity for those on the other side. Hanoun Brass Band‘s “Shamaali / Ya Tal’aeen,” the second track on their debut album From New Orleans to Palestine, takes two songs from that tradition and plays them through New Orleans brass: trumpets, cornets, trombones, saxophones, sousaphone, and percussions. “Tarweedeh Shmaali” is a song about exile and the impossibility of reaching loved ones across an occupied distance, its lyrics encoding that longing through the mlolah technique. “Ya Tal’aeen” was sung by Palestinian women to imprisoned loved ones under Israeli occupation, its coded verses carrying messages of coming liberation. The band’s arrangements are led by accordionist Simon Moushabeck, a Palestinian-American musician who grew up in Massachusetts studying Arabic music and has worked as a professional musician in New Orleans since moving there. Hanoun formed on Twelfth Night, 6 January 2024, when New Orleans musicians and community members marched into the first Carnival parade of the season, filling the route with Arabic drums, brass, and chants for Palestinian liberation. That night became the founding act of New Orleans Musicians for Palestine, an organisation now comprising Hanoun as its community brass band, a Carnival krewe called Krewe of Zeitoun, and a musicians’ solidarity network. From New Orleans to Palestine collects arrangements of Palestinian and Arabic songs the band has played in the streets and at protests over the past two years, all eight tracks arranged for New Orleans brass by Moushabeck, Ashlae Blum’e, and Romain Beauxis, and recorded at the Material Institute in May 2025. Elsewhere on the album: Mohammed Assaf‘s “Ana Dammi Falastini,” a song of Palestinian identity played at protests and weddings across the Arab world; the traditional folk song “Ya Zareef At-Toul,” about longing to leave one’s town, reread now against decades of Palestinian displacement; and “Leve Palestina,” a Swedish song declaring solidarity with Palestinian liberation. Listen to “Shamaali / Ya Tal’aeen” and get your copy of From New Orleans to Palestine HERE. All proceeds from the album go to Gaza Birds Singing, a project supporting music-making in Gaza. The post Daily Discovery: Hanoun Brass Band – Shamaali / Ya Tal‘aeen appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: PIG, the industrial project of English musician Raymond Watts, has announced the PIG “Hurt People Tour”, a North American run of 44 shows in fall 2026 in support of the album “Hurt People Hurt“, released May 22, 2026 via Metropolis Records. The tour starts on August 27 in Lawrence, Kansas and ends on October 18 in Detroit, Michigan. The 44 shows include the band’s previously announced appearances at the Cold Waves XIV festival events in Los Angeles (September 11), Austin (September 18) and Chicago (September 25). An initial 40-date itinerary has been published, with further shows to be added. The August 28 date in Denver is billed with Nitzer Ebb. Ticket links are collected on the band’s official website. Before the North American run, PIG play two previously announced sold-out shows in Tokyo on June 25 and 26, with UK dates to follow in December. PIG ‘Hurt People Tour’ dates: North America fall 2026 Thu, Aug 27 – Lawrence, KS – The Bottleneck Fri, Aug 28 – Denver, CO – Summit (with Nitzer Ebb) Sat, Aug 29 – Salt Lake City, UT – Quarters DLC Mon, Aug 31 – Garden City, ID – Visual Arts Collective Wed, Sept 2 – Spokane, WA – Big Dipper Thu, Sept 3 – Bellingham, WA – The Shakedown Fri, Sept 4 – Seattle, WA – El Corazon Sat, Sept 5 – Portland, OR – Star Theater Mon, Sept 7 – Eugene, OR – John Henry’s Tue, Sept 8 – Eureka, CA – Savage Henry Wed, Sept 9 – Sacramento, CA – Cafe Colonial Thu, Sept 10 – San Francisco, CA – DNA Lounge Fri, Sept 11 – Los Angeles, CA – Cold Waves – Pacific Electric Sat, Sept 12 – Santa Ana, CA – La Santa Sun, Sept 13 – Phoenix, AZ – Last Exit Live Mon, Sept 14 – El Paso, TX – Bye Bye Dear Wed, Sept 16 – Dallas, TX – AM FM Thu, Sept 17 – San Antonio, TX – Paper Tiger Fri, Sept 18 – Austin, TX – Cold Waves – The Mohawk Sat, Sept 19 – Little Rock, AR – Birdie’s Sun, Sept 20 – St. Louis, MO – Red Flag Wed, Sept 23 – Davenport, IA – Raccoon Motel Fri, Sept 25 – Chicago, IL – Cold Waves – The Metro Sat, Sept 26 – Cleveland, OH – Beachland Tavern Sun, Sept 27 – Baltimore, MD – Metro Gallery Tue, Sept 29 – Syracuse, NY – The Song and Dance Thu, Oct 1 – Philadelphia, PA – Nikki Lopez Fri, Oct 2 – Brooklyn, NY – Saint Vitus Sat, Oct 3 – Millersville, PA – Phantom Power Sun, Oct 4 – Richmond, VA – Fallout Mon, Oct 5 – Greenville, SC – Radio Room Wed, Oct 7 – Atlanta, GA – Drunken Unicorn Thu, Oct 8 – Orlando, FL – Conduit Fri, Oct 9 – Tampa, FL – Orpheum Tue, Oct 13 – Columbus, OH – Rumba Wed, Oct 14 – Pittsburgh, PA – Sidequest Thu, Oct 15 – Hamilton, ON – Mill’s Hardware Fri, Oct 16 – Montreal, QC – Toscadura Sat, Oct 17 – Toronto, ON – Lee’s Palace Sun, Oct 18 – Detroit, MI – Smalls ‘Hurt People Hurt’: the album behind the tour “Hurt People Hurt” was released on May 22, 2026 via Metropolis Records on CD, limited edition LP and digital. The 10-track album was largely co-written by Watts with guitarist Jim Davies, known for his work with The Prodigy and Pitchshifter. Two singles preceded it: the first single “Tosca’s Kiss” on March 6, 2026, with a video directed by E Gabriel Edvy. And the second single “Sex & Suicide” on April 10, 2026, with a lyric video directed by Grete Stitch Laus. The album is available via pigindustries.bandcamp.com. About PIG PIG is the long-running industrial rock project of English musician Raymond Watts, which he formed in 1988 after earlier work in London, Hamburg, and West Berlin. Before launching the project, Watts had already worked on early KMFDM material with En Esch and Sascha Konietzko, and had also been active as a live and studio sound engineer for Einstürzende Neubauten and Psychic TV. He later toured with Foetus on keyboards and guitar. The first release was “A Poke in the Eye… with a Sharp Stick”, followed by “Praise the Lard” (1991), “A Stroll in the Pork” (1992), “The Swining” (1993), “Sinsation” (1995), “Wrecked” (1996), “Genuine American Monster” (1999), and “Pigmartyr” (2004), later reissued as “Pigmata”. Small detail, several 1990s releases first appeared in Japan, including “The Swining” and “Wrecked”. Watts is also a founding member and recurring collaborator of KMFDM. He rejoined that orbit in 1994 for the PIG vs KMFDM release “Sin Sex & Salvation”, later worked with the Japanese projects Schaft and Schwein, and also wrote music and sound design for fashion and exhibition work, including Alexander McQueen’s “Plato’s Atlantis” and the Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition “Punk: Chaos to Couture”. After the Watts release “Pigmartyr”, the project resumed under the PIG name with “The Gospel” on September 9, 2016, followed by “Risen” on June 8, 2018 and the covers album “Candy” on June 21, 2019. The project then returned with “Pain Is God” on November 20, 2020, followed by “The Merciless Light” on September 23, 2022. That run continued with “Red Room” on May 17, 2024, the “Feast of Agony” EP on September 27, 2024, the remastered “Wrecked” on March 7, 2025, and the remix album “The Merciful Night” on November 14, 2025. Jim Davies was a recurring collaborator the past few years. And now there is the brand new album “Hurt People Hurt”.

The track is the fourth release in “The Ten Configurations”, the project’s ongoing concept series, and turns its attention to AI companionship. The single is a one-track digital release with a running time of 3:23, davailable on Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer and other streaming platforms. An official visualizer for the track is available as well. Miss Configure’s ‘Token Weighting’ in ‘The Ten Configurations’ series With this single ythe series’ narrative shifts “from algorithmic evaluation to synthetic intimacy”, exploring “how loneliness becomes indexable data and affection turns into a subscription model”, with the track taking what the band calls “a deceptively soft and inviting approach” to the illusion of a “perfect digital companion”. “Token Weighting” follows the singles “Spoiler Alert” (January 9, 2026), “Human_Resources” (February 13, 2026) and “Confidence Score” (May 1, 2026). Earlier singles in the series appeared via None Other Records. About Miss Configure Miss Configure is an audio-visual project built around a digital persona described as an “AI Diva” and “Digital Aristocrat”, created and directed by Warsaw-based producer Jacek Fiszer, who is credited as the project’s “architect”. The project uses generative AI as what it calls a “synthetic co-creator” and applies pop song structures to commentary on automation, digital optimisation and human-AI relations. The project debuted with the single “Spoiler Alert” on January 9, 2026, the first entry in “The Ten Configurations” series. It was followed on February 13, 2026 by “Human_Resources”, which addressed the hidden human labor behind AI systems and content moderation, and on May 1, 2026 by “Confidence Score”, which dealt with algorithmic evaluation. “Token Weighting”, released June 5, 2026, continues the series as its fourth chapter, with a fifth release announced for July 2026.

items.body: Berlin-based dark electro and darkwave duo NNHMN have released the single “Touch Me”. The track previews the eight-track EP “Opera of Lust & the Art of Sorrow II”, due July 15, 2026 on K-Dreams Records on vinyl and as a digital release. The EP can be pre-ordered on Bandcamp, and a video for the track is online as well. Opera of Lust & the Art of Sorrow II by NNHMN ‘Touch Me’ previews ‘Opera of Lust & the Art of Sorrow II’ The duo of Lee and Michal Laudarg presents the single as a warmer counterpoint to the EP’s melancholic side. The other tracks on the EP include “Say my name”, “Touch me”, “Cold like Steel”, “Strange Love”, “Gangster”, “Feelings”, “Mannequin”, and “Golden Crime”. Earlier singles “Say My Name”, “Cold Like Steel”, and “Strange Love” preceded “Touch Me” in the run-up to the release. The EP follows “Opera of Lust & the Art of Sorrow I”, the first chapter in the series. In the May 2026 Side-Line feature NNHMN interview: “We are evolutionists”, Michal Laudarg confirmed the project was already looking past the second part: “Now we are in the world of ‘Opera of Lust and The Art of Sorrow Part Two,’ but the material for the new album already exists.” About NNHMN NNHMN is a Berlin-based dark electronic duo formed by Lee and Michal Laudarg. The project name is read as “non-human”. The pair worked together in earlier projects under different names before starting NNHMN. The album “Church Of No Religion” appeared on the Polish label Zoharum, followed in 2019 by the EP “Shadow In The Dark”, first issued as a limited cassette. In February 2020 the duo launched “Shadow in the Dark” on vinyl through the Spanish label Oraculo Records. The same year brought the “Deception Island” material, including the 12-inch EP “Deception Island Part 1” on Oraculo Records, and a first Side-Line Click Interview with NNHMN. In May 2022 the duo returned with the 4-track EP “For The Comfort Of Your Exstacy” and a video, released via Young and Cold Records and K-Dreams Records. In April 2023 NNHMN re-released previous EPs on one album as “Deception Island 2“, with an extra track. A few singles were released as well: “Your Body”, “Tomorrow’s Heroine”, and “Bring It On”. The “Opera of Lust & the Art of Sorrow” series opened with part one, supported by singles including “Bring It On” and “The Secret”. With “Touch Me”, NNHMN deliver the latest preview of “Opera of Lust & the Art of Sorrow II” before its July 15, 2026 release on K-Dreams Records.

items.body: Two long-deleted studio albums by the German electronic act Rotersand are back in circulation. The Rotersand “Capitalism TM” album from 2016 and “How Do You Feel Today” from 2020 are available again on CD in their Metropolis Records US editions, the distributor Audioglobe announced. The original Trisol editions of both records had been sold out and deleted for years. Rotersand ‘Capitalism TM’ and ‘How Do You Feel Today’: release history “Capitalism TM”, Rotersand’s fifth studio album, was originally released on November 4, 2016 via Trisol and was the band’s first album since “Random Is Resistance” (2009). The 10-track record includes the single “Hey You”, which later lent its title to a full-length remix album. Side-Line covered the original release in 2016 (Rotersand finally hits back with new work: ‘Capitalism TM’) and reviewed it (Rotersand – Capitalism TM (CD Album – Trisol)). “How Do You Feel Today”, the band’s sixth studio album, followed on March 13, 2020 via Trisol, issued both as a vinyl-plus-CD edition and as a regular CD; both editions sold out. The 11-track album contains “Hot Ashes”, “Whatever”, “Silence” and “Elements”, and was reviewed by Side-Line (Rotersand – How Do You Feel Today? (Album – Trisol / Metropolis Records)). The returning US edition is a digipak CD. About Rotersand Rotersand is a German electronic project formed in 2002 by singer Rascal Hüppe and musician/producer Gun, with producer and DJ Krischan J.-E. Wesenberg joining shortly after. The band’s sound is generally described as futurepop, while the members themselves refer to it as “industrial pop”. The debut album “Truth Is Fanatic” appeared in 2003, followed by “Welcome to Goodbye” (2005), “1023” (2007) and “Random Is Resistance” (2009); the first two were reissued in 2021. After “Capitalism TM” (2016) and “How Do You Feel Today” (2020), the latter also reworked as the remix album “Reloaded (Reworks of How Do You Feel Today)” in August 2020, the band released its most recent studio album “Don’t Become The Thing You Hated” in 2025 via Metropolis and Trisol. Side-Line spoke with the band in a 2026 interview. The renewed availability of “Capitalism TM” and “How Do You Feel Today” closes a gap in the band’s catalogue that had persisted since the Trisol pressings sold out.

items.album: San Francisco’s Pont Du Hawk Channels Instrumental Synth and EBM Into Cosmic Machine Dread on “Higher Forces”
items.excerpt: Pont Du Hawk’s Higher Forces comes out of San Francisco like a club record beamed through a military transmitter orbiting some dead moon, ten instrumental tracks of dark electronic dance music with a hard eye on the body and a colder one on the cosmos.
